INT. JACK'S OFFICE - NIGHT

Rain. The old television plays static. Jack sits in the dark, the sketchbook open on the desk.

The black rotary phone RINGS.

He answers. Listens.

KANEKO (V.O.)
(in Japanese; filtered)
Come back. Alone. After the last train.

The line clicks dead.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - NIGHT

Past midnight. The shutter half down. The fluorescent tube is off; only a single bulb burns.

Kaneko lifts the curtain to the storeroom and stands aside.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

Flour sacks. The futon. The bare bulb.

Mara stands against the far wall with a kitchen knife held in both hands. Not well. Her hands are shaking.

Jack stops in the curtain. He holds his hands open where she can see them.

JACK
My name is Jack. Your sister hired me.

MARA
Prove it.

He takes the red bird clip from his pocket. Holds it out on his open palm.

Mara stares at it. The knife lowers an inch.

JACK
She says it was hers. She says you stole it when you were kids and never gave it back.

Something in Mara's face gives way. The knife drops to her side.

MARA
It was never hers. Dad gave it to me. She just says that.

She almost laughs, and then she is crying, silently, pressing the back of her wrist against her mouth.

Jack waits. He doesn't go to her. He sits down on a flour sack, slowly, making himself smaller.

JACK
Is she okay? Is she -- does she know you're --

MARA
Is she okay?

JACK
She's been calling you. She hasn't slept.

MARA
I know. I listen to them.
(beat)
Don't tell her I'm here.

JACK
She's your sister.

MARA
They have my purse. They know my name. They know where I live, where she lives, all of it. If she knows where I am, she'll come here. She won't be able to help it. And they'll follow her.
(beat)
They'll use her to get to me. And then they'll kill her too.

JACK
You don't know that.

MARA
I watched them shoot two men like they were switching off lights.

Silence. The bulb hums.

MARA (CONT'D)
Promise me.

Jack looks at her for a long moment. Twenty years of silence sit behind his eyes.

JACK
I promise.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - DAY

Grey light. Rain on the window. Jack hasn't slept. He is in yesterday's shirt.

Footsteps on the stairs. The frosted glass. Vera's shape.

She comes in carrying two coffees in paper cups. She puts one on his desk.

VERA
You look terrible.

JACK
Thank you.

She sits. She doesn't take her coat off. She waits.

VERA
Did you find anything?

The sketchbook is on the desk between them. Jack's hand rests on its cover.

A train passes. The blinds shiver.

JACK
Not yet.

She nods. Believes him. That's the worst part.

VERA
Okay.
(beat)
Okay. Tomorrow, then.

She stands. At the door she hesitates, as though she wants to say something else. She doesn't. She goes.

Jack sits very still. He picks up the coffee she brought him and holds it without drinking, the way he held the can at the vending machine.

INT. ALL-NIGHT NOODLE COUNTER, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

A different place: a narrow standing-and-stools counter wedged into a brick railway arch. A ticket machine by the door. Yellowed menus on the wall. A radio behind the counter plays baseball, low.

11:40 p.m. by the clock over the door.

Vera and Jack sit side by side at the counter. Empty bowls. Two coffees in thick white cups. They have been here a long time.

Every few minutes, a train rumbles overhead, and the cups tremble in their saucers.

VERA
He used to bring us somewhere like this. Dad. After work. Mara would fall asleep on the counter and he'd carry her home.

JACK
And you?

VERA
I stayed awake. I wanted to hear everything he said to the man who made the noodles. I didn't understand any of it. I just liked that he was different here. Lighter.
(beat)
I think he was happy here. Before.

Jack looks down at his cup.

VERA (CONT'D)
They said he killed himself. My mother never talked about it. Not once. We went home and it was as if Tokyo never happened.

JACK
Do you believe it?

She thinks about it for a long time.

VERA
I believe he was sad. I don't know if I believe the rest.

A train. The cups tremble.

VERA (CONT'D)
You're very easy to talk to. It's annoying.

JACK
I get paid to listen.

VERA
You're not getting paid right now.

He has no answer to that.

She rests her head on her folded arms on the counter. Just for a moment. Her eyes close.

VERA (CONT'D)
(barely awake)
You're the first person I've trusted since she disappeared. Did you know that?

Jack looks at her. His mouth opens. The truth is right there.

JACK
Vera --

But she is asleep.

He sits and watches her breathe. A train passes. Her coffee cup, near her elbow, trembles toward the edge of the counter.

He reaches over and moves it back from the edge. Carefully. Quietly. So it won't wake her.

He doesn't wake her. He sits there until the counterman begins stacking chairs.

EXT. YAKITORI STALL, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

Smoke. Red paper lanterns. Salarymen at plastic tables under a railway bridge, talking too loud.

Ishida sits alone at a corner table with a beer and a plate of skewers. Jack sits down opposite him.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
You never call me unless you want something.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Sakai.

Ishida sighs. Turns a skewer over with his chopsticks.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
You already know what he was. In the bubble years he cleared land. Old tenants who wouldn't sell. First he'd bring flowers. Then he'd bring men. Then something would happen. A fire, sometimes.

JACK
(in Japanese)
The Shiohama fire.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Among others.
(beat)
The journalist in the bar was from the Toto Shimbun. He'd been asking about the redevelopment money. Who owns what. Whose friends vote on what. The usual. Sakai called him a week ago. We think Sakai wanted to confess something before he died. He had cancer. Months left.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Confess what?

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Who knows. An old man's conscience. It's very common.

Jack watches him.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Why are you telling me all this?

Ishida puts down his chopsticks.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Because you'll find out anyway. And because I would rather you heard it from me than from someone who wants to hurt you.
(beat)
Twenty years ago I told you to sign that report. You were young. You did what your senior told you. That was on me, not on you.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I still signed it.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
And I've carried it too. Every day.
(beat)
Whatever Sakai hid, Jack, if you find it, bring it to me. Not to the department. To me. I'll know what to do with it this time.

A long pause. A train roars overhead. The lanterns sway.

Jack nods slowly.

It is exactly what he needed to hear. That is what makes it dangerous.

INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - NIGHT

The fortieth floor. Glass on three sides. Tokyo spread out below in the rain like a circuit board.

Silence. Thick carpet. A single orchid.

In the centre of the room, under a glass case: an architectural model of the redevelopment. White towers, green parks, tiny white trees. Where the Hive stands now, there is a plaza with a fountain.

THE CHAIRMAN, KUROSE (70s), stands at the window with his hands behind his back. Silver hair. A beautiful suit. The stillness of a man who has never had to hurry.

Behind him, near the door, stands the MASKED LEADER, unmasked here: a man in his forties in a plain dark suit, a face you would forget immediately. He is the man who touched his earpiece in the rain.

MASKED LEADER
(in Japanese)
The detective went into the Hive twice. Once in the day. Once after the last train.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
And?

MASKED LEADER
(in Japanese)
We can't follow him in there. Too many people. Too many passages. They see everyone.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
Then don't follow him in there.

He turns from the window.

KUROSE (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Let the detective look. He was always very good at finding things.
(beat)
It's what he does afterwards that he's bad at.

He looks down at the model. At the little plaza where the Hive will be. He straightens one tiny white tree with the tip of his finger.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

The bulb. The flour sacks. Mara sits cross-legged on the futon, a bowl of rice going cold in her lap. Jack sits against the opposite wall. They talk quietly, as if the building is listening. It is.

MARA
The old man said "twenty years." Before they shot him. Like he'd been expecting them for twenty years.

JACK
He probably had.

MARA
And then in the bar, the man said, "Where is he?" He was waiting for the old man. They were supposed to meet.

JACK
Sakai was bringing him something.

Mara opens her fist. The coin-locker key on its worn plastic tag.

MARA
This.

Jack takes it. Turns it over under the bulb. A number stamped into the metal: 114. The plastic tag is so old the printing has worn away.

JACK
It's not a station locker. They clear those every three days.

MARA
Then what is it?

JACK
Somewhere he paid for. For a long time.

He hands it back. She looks surprised.

JACK (CONT'D)
Keep it. Until I know what it opens. It's safer with you than with me.

MARA
Why?

JACK
Because nobody knows where you are.

Mara closes her hand around the key. She looks at him properly for the first time.

MARA
Is she eating?

JACK
What?

MARA
Vera. She forgets to eat when she's upset. She just drinks coffee. Is she eating?

Jack thinks of the counter at 11:40 p.m. The empty bowls.

JACK
Last night she had noodles.

MARA
Good.
(beat)
Make her eat breakfast. She never eats breakfast.

INT. YAMANOTE LINE TRAIN - DAY

A green-striped commuter train circling the city. Rain on the windows. Afternoon light, grey and soft. The carriage is half empty: schoolkids, an old man asleep, a woman with shopping.

Vera and Jack sit side by side. Nowhere to go. Just riding the loop.

VERA
Dad used to do this when he couldn't think. Ride the whole loop. An hour. He said Tokyo was a clock and the Yamanote was the second hand.

JACK
Did it help?

VERA
I don't know. He did it a lot at the end.

The train sways. Her shoulder settles against his.

She takes his hand without asking and turns it over. The old steel lighter is in his palm; he has been flicking it without knowing.

She takes it. Opens it. Closes it. Opens it.

VERA (CONT'D)
You don't smoke.

JACK
I quit.

VERA
When?

JACK
Twenty years ago.

VERA
And you still carry the lighter.

JACK
Habit.

VERA
That's not a habit. That's a promise you don't trust yourself to keep.

He looks at her. She has no idea how true that is.

She tries to give it back. He closes her fingers around it.

JACK
Keep it.

VERA
Why?

JACK
Because I quit.

She looks at the lighter in her hand. Then she puts it in her coat pocket. And her head comes to rest on his shoulder, as if it has always belonged there.

Out of the window, Tokyo circles past. Rooftops. Laundry. Rain.

EXT. PEDESTRIAN CROSSING - DAY

A small intersection. The crossing signal turns green and the old melody begins to CHIME.

Vera and Jack cross in the rain, laughing at something, sharing his cheap plastic umbrella that's too small for two. Her shoulder gets wet. His gets wet. Neither of them cares.

WIDE: two small figures crossing an empty road while the city's old song plays for them.

EXT. FISHING TOWN, BOSO COAST - DAY

Grey sea. Grey sky. Boats pulled up on a concrete slipway. A single road of low houses, their paint scoured by salt wind.

Jack's old car, parked on the sea wall. He gets out, pulls up his collar against the wind, and walks.

INT. MRS. SAKAI'S HOUSE - DAY

A small room. A kotatsu table. A television with the sound off. A Buddhist altar in the corner: a new photograph of Sakai, younger, smiling in a way that doesn't suit him.

MRS. SAKAI (70s), small and hard, pours Jack tea she doesn't want to pour.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
We haven't lived together in fifteen years. The police already came.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm not the police.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
Then what are you?

Jack thinks about it.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Someone who owes a man a debt. A long time ago. The same kind of debt your husband owed.

She studies him. Then she looks at the photograph on the altar.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
He started going to temple last year. Him. Temple. He sat there for hours. I thought he'd gone soft in the head.
(beat)
When the doctor told him, he said he was glad. He said now he could stop being afraid of the wrong thing.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Did he ever pay rent on something? Somewhere that wasn't his home?

She looks at him sharply.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
Every January. Cash, in an envelope. Twenty years. Even the years we had nothing, he paid it. I thought it was a woman.

She gets up, goes to a drawer, comes back with a thin bundle of old receipts held together with a rubber band. Carbon copies, handwritten, yellowed. She puts them in front of Jack.

MRS. SAKAI (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
He left these here. Maybe on purpose.

Jack unfolds the top one. A rubber stamp, faded: KATO RENTAL LOCKERS - UENO. Handwritten: No. 114. Paid in full.

He looks up. She is watching him with an expression he can't read. Grief, maybe. Or relief.

MRS. SAKAI (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Whatever it is, it was heavier than me. He carried it longer.


EXT. COUNTRY HIGHWAY - NIGHT

Rain. Black fields. Jack's old car, one headlight dimmer than the other, the only thing moving for miles.

Ahead, a light. A sign on a pole, half its bulbs dead: a roadside inn.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN - NIGHT

Two storeys of weathered wood and a tin roof, set back from the highway behind a gravel lot. A beer vending machine glowing by the entrance. A faded sign. The kind of place that was modern once, in about 1975.

A pickup truck, older than the building's paint, is parked crooked behind it.

Jack pulls into the lot. The only car.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

A small, warm, faded room. A pink public payphone on the wall. A glass case of souvenir keyrings nobody has bought in decades. A CRT television on a shelf showing a night baseball game, the crowd murmuring.

MRS. NODA (70s) comes out from the back, drying her hands. MR. NODA (70s) doesn't look away from the baseball.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Just one night?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Just one.

She hands him a heavy old key on a wooden tag.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Upstairs, at the end. The bath is shared, I'm sorry. I'll show you. The light doesn't work properly.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, CORRIDOR AND BATH - CONTINUOUS

She leads him down a narrow wooden corridor. Past the kitchen: pots, a steel counter, a back door with a bolt.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Kitchen. If you want tea, just take it. The back door sticks. My husband says he'll fix it. He's said so since the Olympics.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Which Olympics?

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Exactly.

She opens a door: a small tiled bathroom, a deep wooden tub, one high window over it, fogged with steam and swollen shut in its frame.

MRS. NODA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
If it's too steamy, the window opens. If you hit it hard enough.

Jack notices the window. He notices everything. That is the point of the scene, and nobody in it knows it.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, JACK'S ROOM - NIGHT

Tatami. A low table. A thin futon already laid out. Rain loud on the tin roof.

Jack sits at the table with Sakai's receipts spread out in front of him under the lamp. KATO RENTAL LOCKERS - UENO. No. 114. Twenty years of Januaries.

He takes out his phone. No signal.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - NIGHT

Mr. Noda asleep in front of the baseball. Jack at the pink payphone, feeding it coins.

INTERCUT WITH:

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - NIGHT

Vera on the floor with her back against the bed, the apartment dark around her. Her phone rings. Unknown number. She answers fast.

VERA
Mara?

JACK (V.O.)
It's me.

A beat. Disappointment, then something else.

VERA
Where are you? You sound like you're calling from 1985.

JACK
The countryside. There's no signal. I'm on a payphone. It's pink.

She almost laughs.

VERA
Did you find anything?

Jack looks at the receipts in his hand.

JACK
Maybe. I'll know tomorrow.

VERA
Come back safe.

JACK
It's just an inn. There's an old couple and a baseball game.

VERA
Come back safe anyway.

He hears her breathing on the line. Neither of them hangs up.

The coins run out. The line goes dead.

Vera looks at the phone. Jack looks at the payphone. Both of them hold on a moment longer than they need to.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN DOORWAY - NIGHT

Jack can't sleep. He wanders back down the corridor.

The kitchen's back door stands open to the rain. Mrs. Noda sits on the step outside under the eave, smoking.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Don't tell my husband.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I quit.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Then you'll understand why I don't want him to know.

She offers the pack anyway. He shakes his head. He stands in the doorway and looks out: a muddy yard, a gate onto a farm track, and the old pickup parked crooked across the path.

MRS. NODA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Sorry about the truck. He parks it like he's drunk. He's never drunk. The keys are always in it. Who would steal that?

Jack looks at the truck. He says nothing.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN - NIGHT

Later. 2 a.m. Rain.

The highway. Empty. Then headlights.

One car. Two. Three. Four. Black sedans, one after another, slowing, turning in, gravel crunching.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, JACK'S ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Jack's eyes open in the dark. He has heard the gravel.

He goes to the window. Lifts one corner of the thin curtain.

HIS POV THROUGH THE CURTAIN GAP: four black cars in an arc across the lot, headlights on, rain visible only inside the beams. Eight MEN step out, two from each car. Black clothes. Masks. Compact submachine guns held low and easy.

They don't rush. They split without speaking. Two toward the entrance. Two around the back. Two toward the side. Two stay by the cars.

Jack lets the curtain fall.

He moves fast and quietly: sweeps the receipts into his jacket, pulls on his shoes, takes nothing else.

Downstairs, the baseball crowd CHEERS on the TV.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

The front door opens. Two masked men step in, weapons up.

Mr. Noda wakes in his chair. Stares.

MR. NODA
(in Japanese)
We're closed --

A burst of suppressed fire into the ceiling. Plaster rains down. Mr. Noda throws himself behind the counter.

The souvenir case shatters. The CRT keeps playing baseball.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, UPSTAIRS CORRIDOR - CONTINUOUS

Jack at the top of the stairs. He hears boots below. He goes the other way, toward the bath.

Behind him, a masked man reaches the top of the stairs and fires down the corridor. The paper screens along one wall burst apart in a line of holes.

Jack is already through the bathroom door.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, BATHROOM - CONTINUOUS

Dark. Steam still hanging. Jack climbs onto the edge of the deep tub and hits the swollen window frame with the heel of his hand. Once. Twice. It won't move.

Boots in the corridor.

The third time, he hits it with everything he has. The frame cracks open. Rain pours in.

He hauls himself through.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN ROOF - CONTINUOUS

A low slope of wet tin below the bathroom window. Jack drops onto it, slides, catches the gutter, and swings down --

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN - CONTINUOUS

-- through the open back door into the kitchen, where Mrs. Noda is crouched on the floor behind the steel counter, rigid with fear.

He grabs her arm, pulls her low toward the pantry, opens it, puts her inside.

JACK
(in Japanese; whispered)
Stay. Whatever you hear.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese; whispered)
My husband --

JACK
(in Japanese; whispered)
I'll get him.

He closes the pantry door on her.

He moves up the corridor toward the lobby, keeping low along the wall.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

From the corridor, Jack can see the lobby. One masked man stands in the middle of the room, weapon up, covering the stairs. The other has gone up.

Mr. Noda is behind the counter, out of the gunman's line of sight. He sees Jack. Jack puts a finger to his lips.

Jack reaches out and flips the lobby light switch. DARK.

Only the TV lights the room now: blue, flickering.

The masked man spins and fires toward the corridor. The shots stitch across the wall above Jack's head. One tears through the beer vending machine by the door.

It lights up and CHIMES:

VENDING MACHINE
(recorded; in Japanese)
Thank you very much.

The gunman flinches toward the sound.

In that half-second, Jack is across the dark lobby, behind the counter. He grabs Mr. Noda by the collar and drags him down the corridor.

On the wall, the pink payphone starts to RING.

No one answers it. It rings and rings.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN - CONTINUOUS

Jack pushes Mr. Noda into the pantry beside his wife. The old couple clutch each other in the dark.

Jack looks at them.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm sorry.

He shuts the door. He goes out the back.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, BACK YARD - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Mud. The farm gate. The pickup truck.

A masked man comes round the side of the building. Sees him.

Jack runs. Gunfire kicks up mud behind him. He dives behind the truck. Bullets punch through the bodywork above his head, through the tailgate, through a wheel.

He yanks open the driver's door and pulls himself in, flat along the seat.

INT. PICKUP TRUCK - CONTINUOUS

The keys are in the ignition, exactly where she said.

He turns them. The engine coughs. Dies.

The windscreen cracks as a round goes through it.

JACK
(under his breath)
Come on. Come on.

He turns the key again. The engine catches. Roars.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, BACK YARD - CONTINUOUS

The truck lurches forward and smashes through the farm gate. Two masked men throw themselves aside. The truck fishtails through the mud onto the farm track, then onto the highway.

The eight men walk out into the lot, one by one, and stand in the headlights of their cars, watching the single red taillight shrink into the rain.

They don't chase him. They don't need to.

The MASKED LEADER touches his earpiece.

MASKED LEADER
(in Japanese)
He's gone. He has what she gave him.

Behind them, inside the lobby, the pink payphone is still ringing.

INT. PICKUP TRUCK - MOVING - DAWN

Grey light. Empty highway. Rain through the shattered windscreen.

Jack drives with one hand. Blood runs from his hairline down the side of his face. His shirt is dark with it at the shoulder.

He looks in the mirror. No one.

He reaches into his jacket. The receipts are still there, soaked and creased.

He breathes. Only now does his hand start to shake.

Then the thought arrives, and his face changes.

Only two people knew where he was going tonight. He counts them silently.

Ishida. He asked Ishida for the widow's address.

And Vera. He called her from a pink payphone and told her it was just an inn.

He drives on. The wipers beat. He doesn't want to think it. He thinks it anyway.

INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAWN

The glass walls grey with dawn. Kurose sits in a leather chair beside the model of the redevelopment, a cup of tea on the arm of the chair.

Standing before him, hat in hand, raincoat still wet: Detective ISHIDA.

It is the first time we see them together. It explains everything.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
I told you. Leave him alone. Let him find it.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
You told me he was tired, Ishida. That he had given up twenty years ago. He doesn't look tired to me.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
He trusts me. He'll bring it to me. He said so.
(beat)
Then we take both. The girl and the thing.

Kurose sips his tea. He looks down at the model: the little plaza with its fountain where the Hive still stands.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
You were always very careful. I hope you still are.

Ishida bows. Holds the bow a moment too long.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - DAWN

A knock at the door. Vera opens it in a sweater, barely awake.

Jack. Soaked. Blood dried down the side of his face.

VERA
Oh my God.

She pulls him in.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT, BATHROOM - CONTINUOUS

A small tiled bathroom. Jack sits on the closed toilet. Vera kneels in front of him with a bowl of warm water and a cloth, cleaning the cut at his hairline.

He watches her face while she works. Very closely. As though he is trying to read something written there.

VERA
Who did this?

JACK
I don't know.

VERA
You don't know?

JACK
Eight men. Masks. They didn't introduce themselves.

She wrings out the cloth. Pink water.

VERA
You told me it was just an inn.

JACK
It was just an inn.

She looks up and catches him watching her.

VERA
What?

He doesn't answer. He's still watching. Measuring. She sees something in his look that she doesn't understand, and it frightens her more than the blood.

VERA (CONT'D)
Jack. What?

He looks at her hands: careful, steady, stained pink. At her face: exhausted, afraid for him.

Whatever he was looking for, it isn't there. It was never there.

JACK
Nothing.
(beat)
I'm sorry. Nothing.

She puts a plaster on the cut, very gently. Her hand stays on his face a moment after.

He covers her hand with his.

And then, without either of them deciding, she kisses him. Or he kisses her. It doesn't matter which.

It is quiet, and brief, and it changes everything.

When it ends, she rests her forehead against his.

VERA
Don't go anywhere else without telling me.

JACK
I won't.

It is another promise. He is collecting them.

EXT. OLD TOBACCO KIOSK - DAY

A tiny kiosk wedged into the corner of a shopping arcade. An OLD TOBACCONIST (80s) behind a window full of cigarette cartons and lottery tickets.

Vera holds up the old photograph. The American man, two small girls, the noodle shop sign.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My father worked near here, a long time ago. Do you know this place?

The tobacconist puts on his glasses. Looks. Smiles with all his remaining teeth.

OLD TOBACCONIST
(in Japanese)
Kaneko's. Of course. In the Hive.
(beat)
Not for long, though. They're knocking it all down.

Vera stares at him.

VERA
(in Japanese)
It's still there?

OLD TOBACCONIST
(in Japanese)
Everything is still there. Until it isn't.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - DAY

Vera walks through the narrow corridors with the photograph in her hand, looking at everything as though she's trying to remember it. Bare bulbs. Dripping water. The radio repairman's dozen murmuring stations.

A train passes overhead. The building trembles.

She stops. Turns a corner.

The noodle counter. The sign.

She stands there for a long moment, holding the photograph up beside the real thing. They match.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Lunchtime. Steam. Three customers.

Vera sits on the third stool.

Kaneko turns from the pot, sees her, and freezes. Just for a second. Then she goes on working.

VERA
(in Japanese)
I'm sorry, I don't know what to order. I was here when I was a child. With my father. He always sat here.

Kaneko looks at her for a long moment.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
He always paid too much.

Vera's breath catches.

VERA
(in Japanese)
You remember him?

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
And you. You ate everything on his plate.

She sets a bowl of noodles in front of Vera. Vera looks at it. Her eyes fill.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

On the other side of the curtain, three feet away.

Mara stands pressed against the wall with both hands over her mouth. She has heard her sister's voice. She is shaking.

Through the thin gap at the edge of the curtain she can see the back of Vera's head. The third stool.

Mara takes one step toward the curtain. Her hand lifts to it.

She stops.

She thinks of the purse in the rain. Of the two men falling. Of her sister being followed through these corridors.

Her hand drops.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Vera eats. All of it. She laughs once, at nothing, wiping her eyes.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister would love this place. She's never seen it. She only knows it from my stories.
(beat)
When I find her, I'll bring her here.

Kaneko's chopsticks stop moving in the pot. She doesn't look up.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Yes. Bring her.

Vera puts money on the counter. Too much. Kaneko notices and says nothing.

Vera goes, lighter than she has been for the whole film.

Behind the curtain, Mara slides down the wall to the floor.

EXT. THE HIVE - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Vera comes out of the Hive's narrow entrance, glowing.

Jack is coming the other way, fast, soaked. He sees her. He stops dead.

VERA
Jack! It's still here. The noodle shop from the photo. It's real. The same woman -- she remembered Dad. She remembered me.

She is so happy. She throws her arms around him.

Over her shoulder, Jack looks at the entrance of the Hive. At the street. At the rain. At every parked car.

VERA (CONT'D)
When we find Mara, I'm bringing her here. She'll finally see it.

JACK
(quietly)
Yes.

He holds her. His face, over her shoulder, is the face of a man at the edge of a very high place.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

The bulb. Mara sits on the futon with her knees pulled up. Her face is swollen from crying. Jack crouches in front of her.

MARA
She was right there. She was right there and I --

JACK
You did the right thing.

MARA
Did I?
(beat)
She said she'd bring me here. When she finds me. She was so happy.

She wipes her face with the heel of her hand.

JACK
If she found this place, other people can.

MARA
I know.

She opens her hand. The key. Number 114.

MARA (CONT'D)
Find what it opens. And then this ends. I don't want to hide any more. I want my sister.

Jack takes the key.

JACK
Tomorrow night I'm moving you out of here. Somewhere safe, outside Tokyo. A police car and a house. Someone I trust.

MARA
And then?

JACK
And then I tell her everything.

Mara looks at him. She believes him.

INT. ISHIDA'S CAR - NIGHT

Parked under an elevated expressway. Rain drumming on the roof. The dashboard glow.

Ishida behind the wheel. Jack in the passenger seat. Neither looks at the other.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I have a witness. From the bar.

A pause. Ishida's expression doesn't change at all. That is the tell, and only we know it.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
The sister.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I need a safe car. A safe house outside the city. No paperwork. No department. Just you.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
When?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Tomorrow night.

Ishida nods slowly, as if thinking it through. As if it costs him something.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Nine o'clock. The service road behind the Hive, by the railway pillars. A grey car. My driver. I'll arrange the house myself.
(beat)
And Sakai's thing?

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'll bring it to you. When she's safe.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Good.
(beat)
You've done well, Jack. This time you've done well.

Jack looks out at the rain. For the first time in twenty years, he lets himself believe it.

EXT. PEDESTRIAN CROSSING - NIGHT

The same small intersection as before. The signal is red. Vera and Jack stand at the kerb under his cheap plastic umbrella.

JACK
Tomorrow night. Will you have dinner with me?

She looks at him, surprised.

VERA
Like a date?

JACK
Like a date.

VERA
Jack, my sister --

JACK
I know.
(beat)
There's something I need to tell you. I want to tell you properly. Not in an office. Not on a train.

She searches his face. Whatever she finds there makes her smile. Properly. For the first time in the film.

VERA
Okay.

JACK
The old hotel by the station. The lounge. Ten o'clock.

VERA
Ten o'clock.

The signal turns green. The old melody begins to CHIME.

They cross. She takes his arm.

INT. KATO RENTAL LOCKERS, UENO - NIGHT

A narrow room under a railway arch, lined floor to ceiling with battered grey steel lockers, each one numbered in fading paint. A single fluorescent tube. A sign in faded letters: MONTHLY. YEARLY. NO QUESTIONS.

At a desk by the door, a CARETAKER (80s) sleeps with his head on a ledger.

Jack walks the rows. 98. 106. 112. 114.

He fits the key. It turns stiffly, as though it hasn't turned in years.

The door creaks open.

Inside: a small cardboard box, softened with age. Jack lifts the lid.

A single cassette tape in a cracked plastic case, labelled in a shaking hand: SHIOHAMA. And beneath it, a notebook with a worn cloth cover.

Jack opens the notebook. English handwriting. Neat, slanted, careful. Dates. Names. Diagrams of a burned building.

On the inside cover: DANIEL VOSS.

Jack stands very still.

He turns pages. The handwriting grows faster, more anxious. And then a page near the end, and a line underlined twice.

He reads it. We don't see what it says. We see his face.

He closes the notebook.

A train passes overhead. The lockers rattle in their rows, all of them at once, like a room full of doors being tried.

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - NIGHT

Okada's bar. Late. No customers. The CRT television is off.

Jack slides the cassette case across the counter.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Keep this for me. Don't tell anyone. Not the police. Not me, if I ask you with someone standing behind me.

Okada looks at the tape. Then he takes it, lifts the lid of the old cash drawer, removes the tray, and puts the tape underneath.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
Behind the counter. Like the girl's clip.

He pours Jack a drink. Jack doesn't drink it.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Tomorrow it'll be over.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
That's what people say the night before.


INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - EVENING

Rain on the window. The last grey light.

Vera stands on a chair and lifts down a flat cardboard box from the top of the wardrobe. Dust on the lid. Her mother's handwriting on the side, in marker: TOKYO.

She opens it on the bed.

Inside, folded in tissue paper that has gone yellow: a dress. Wine red. Silk. The kind of dress a young woman wore to an expensive restaurant in 1990 and never wore again.

Vera holds it up against herself in the mirror. For a moment she is someone else. Her mother, maybe.

Through the thin wall, the neighbour's radio begins to play the same old ballad from before: the woman's voice, the slow saxophone.

LATER:

Vera at the small mirror by the window, in the red dress, doing her makeup. She is out of practice. She wipes off the lipstick and does it again. Her hands aren't quite steady.

She looks at herself for a long time. She almost looks happy. She doesn't quite trust it.

She picks up her bag. Puts in her phone. Then, after a moment, the old steel lighter.

At the door she stops by the umbrella stand. The pale blue umbrella.

She takes it.

VERA
(quietly, to the empty room)
Borrowing it. You'll get it back.

She goes. Through the wall, the song plays on.

INT. HOTEL LOUNGE - NIGHT

An old hotel built in the Showa years for a future that never quite came. Amber light. Brass rails. Deep leather chairs. Bottles glowing behind the bar like a shrine.

In the corner, a PIANIST (60s) in a white jacket plays standards, softly, to almost no one.

A clock above the bar: 9:58.

Vera comes in, shaking the rain from the blue umbrella. People turn to look at her, briefly. She is beautiful and doesn't know where to put her hands.

She sits at the bar. Leans the blue umbrella against the next stool.

BARTENDER
(in Japanese)
For you?

VERA
(in Japanese)
I'm waiting for someone.
(beat)
A gin and tonic. Please.

She looks at the door.

The clock: 10:00.

EXT. SERVICE ROAD BEHIND THE HIVE - NIGHT

Earlier. The clock is a different clock here: 8:52 on a lit sign above a closed garage.

A narrow road running under the elevated railway. A row of massive concrete pillars. Puddles. One sodium lamp.

A grey sedan waits beside the pillars, engine running, wipers slow.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

Mara puts on a borrowed coat. She has a small cloth bag: a toothbrush, the cardigan, the sketchbook pages she tore from the wall.

Kaneko stands in the curtain. She hands Mara a small parcel wrapped in newspaper.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Rice balls. For the car.

Mara takes them. She doesn't know what to say.

MARA
(in halting Japanese)
Thank you. For --

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Come back with your sister. Sit on the stools. Both of you. Eat everything.

Mara bows, too deep, clumsy. Kaneko, unexpectedly, puts a hand on her head. Just for a second. Like a grandmother.

JACK (O.S.)
It's time.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - NIGHT

Jack leads Mara through the narrow corridors. Bare bulbs. Dripping pipes. The radio repairman looks up from his bench as they pass, and nods.

Doors open onto other lives. A family watching television. A man asleep. A girl practising the violin, badly.

Mara looks at all of it as if memorising it.

MARA
Vera would love this.

JACK
You can bring her.

MARA
When it's over, you'll tell her? Everything?

JACK
Tonight. I'm meeting her at ten.

She stops walking. Looks at him.

MARA
Meeting her?

JACK
For dinner.

Mara studies him. And then, for the first time, she smiles. A real one. Her sister's smile.

MARA
Oh. Oh, I see.

JACK
It's not --

MARA
It is. It's fine. It's good.
(beat)
She deserves someone who looks for things.

A train passes overhead. The building trembles. They walk on.

EXT. SERVICE ROAD BEHIND THE HIVE - CONTINUOUS

Jack and Mara come out of a narrow back door of the Hive into the rain.

The grey sedan waits beside the pillars, twenty metres away. A DRIVER in a dark coat gets out and opens the rear door for them. Polite. Professional.

Jack walks Mara toward it. Halfway there.

The driver lifts his wrist to his mouth and murmurs into his sleeve, very quietly:

DRIVER
(in Japanese)
Position.

Mara stops dead.

She has heard that word before. In the rain. Over a dying man.

MARA
(whispering)
That's them.

JACK
What?

MARA
That's what they said. Position. That's them.

Jack looks at the driver. The driver looks at Jack. And in that look, both men understand.

Jack shoves Mara back toward the Hive door.

JACK
Run!

From the dark between the pillars: muzzle flashes. Suppressed shots, flat and ordinary.

Jack draws Mara down behind a dumpster. Rounds clang off the steel. The driver pulls a weapon from his coat.

Mara breaks for the Hive door. Five metres. Three.

A shot.

She stumbles. Keeps going. Falls through the doorway.

Jack goes after her, low, as bullets chew the doorframe above his head.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGE - CONTINUOUS

Jack drags the door shut behind him and throws the bolt. Pounding on the door. Shots through it, splintering the wood.

Mara is on the floor of the narrow passage, her back against the wall. She is holding her side. Her hand is dark and wet.

Jack kneels, presses his hands over hers.

JACK
Stay with me. Mara. Stay with me.

Above them, a window opens. Then another. Doors bang open along the passage. Voices. Lights snap on, one after another, up through the whole building: the thousand windows of the Hive waking.

The RADIO REPAIRMAN runs into the passage with a flashlight. The FAMILY'S FATHER behind him with a baseball bat. Kaneko, in her apron.

Outside, a car door slams. An engine revs. Tyres on wet asphalt. Going.

And far away, finally, sirens.

Mara looks up at all the light.

MARA
Everyone's awake.

JACK
Yes. Everyone's awake. Help's coming.

Mara's hand finds his wrist. Her grip is weak.

MARA
Jack.

JACK
I'm here.

MARA
Tell her I'm sorry.

JACK
You'll tell her. Tonight. I'll bring her here, you can --

MARA
Tell her.

Her eyes stay on the lights above. Then they stop moving.

Jack doesn't let go of her hand.

Kaneko sinks down beside them in the narrow passage. She doesn't cry. She takes off her apron and folds it and places it gently under Mara's head, as though that still matters.

A train passes overhead. The bulbs swing. The whole building trembles, the way it always does.

INT. HOTEL LOUNGE - NIGHT

The clock above the bar: 11:52.

Vera's gin and tonic sits untouched. The ice has melted. The lime has sunk.

The pianist plays something slow. The same old ballad from the neighbour's radio, only now on a piano, stripped of its words.

Vera looks at the door. At her phone. No messages.

She takes out the lighter and turns it over in her fingers. Open. Shut.

BARTENDER
(in Japanese)
Another?

VERA
(in Japanese)
No. Thank you.

She almost laughs at herself. She looks down at the red dress. She feels foolish, and then hurt, and then angry.

Her phone RINGS.

She grabs it. The screen: ISHIDA.

Her face changes. She answers.

VERA (CONT'D)
Hello?

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(filtered; gently)
Miss Voss. I'm so sorry to call so late.

She knows. From his voice, she already knows. She stands up.

ISHIDA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Your sister was found tonight. I'm very sorry. She died a short time ago.

Vera doesn't move. The piano plays on.

ISHIDA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
She was with Mr. Jack. He had been hiding her for several days, it seems. In the Hive.
(beat)
I'm sorry. I thought you knew.

The phone slowly lowers from her ear.

The pianist plays. The clock ticks. Somewhere a glass is set down.

Vera walks out of the lounge. Not running yet. Walking very carefully, as if the floor might give way.

The blue umbrella stays where she left it, leaning against the empty stool.

EXT. TOKYO STREETS - NIGHT

Vera comes out of the hotel into the rain and starts to run.

Not elegantly. Badly. In heels, in the red dress, no coat, no umbrella. Slipping. Stumbling. Stopping for half a second because she can't breathe, then forcing herself on.

Rain plasters her hair to her face. Her mascara runs.

No music. Only rain. Her heels on wet pavement. Her breath. A car passing, its tyres hissing.

She runs past a vending machine. It glows, indifferent.

At a crossing, the old melody chimes for her, and she runs through it on red.

One heel skids. Her ankle turns. The shoe comes off and stays behind in a puddle. She doesn't stop. She runs on in one shoe.

EXT. EMPTY STREET UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

A long, empty street beside the elevated railway. Shuttered shops. A row of vending machines, their cold white light the only light, rain falling through it in columns. The black road shining like water.

In a city of fourteen million people, no one else is here.

Jack walks out of the dark from the direction of the Hive. His coat is soaked. His hands are dark. He has not washed them.

He sees her at the far end of the street.

He stops under the awning of a closed shop.

Vera slows. Stops. Twenty metres apart.

For a moment neither of them says anything. She is crying, almost silently.

Jack takes one step toward her.

She shakes her head.

VERA
Don't.

He stops.

She looks at him. There is something almost childlike in her face now. Not rage. Disbelief. As though she is still hoping he will tell her that what she's heard is wrong.

She walks toward him. Slowly. One shoe, one bare foot on the wet road.

VERA (CONT'D)
You knew.

Jack doesn't answer.

Her face changes. That silence is the answer.

She hits him. Not a big cinematic slap. One desperate blow against his chest with her fist.

He takes it.

She hits him again. Then again.

VERA (CONT'D)
You knew where she was.

He says nothing. He can't. Behind his silence is a promise to a dead girl, and the audience knows it, and Vera doesn't.

She hits him again, weaker. And then the anger drains out of her all at once. Her hands just fall.

VERA (CONT'D)
(whispering)
Why didn't you tell me?

Jack opens his mouth. Nothing comes.

VERA (CONT'D)
She was waiting for me.

That line is almost inaudible.

Jack looks away.

VERA (CONT'D)
And I was waiting for you.
(beat)
And you were with her.

Jack closes his eyes.

And that is when Vera finally breaks. Not screaming. She simply folds. Her knees hit the wet pavement.

Jack drops down instinctively, reaching for her.

Her hands grab the front of his coat. She holds on. For one second it looks as if she is going to let him hold her.

Then she realises whose coat it is.

She pushes him away.

And sits there, in the rain, in the red dress.

Jack kneels a few feet away. He doesn't touch her again.

WIDE. EXTREME WIDE.

Two small figures on a huge, empty, shining street. The vending machines hum. The rain falls through their light.

Every sound drops away except the rain.

In the black water beside Vera, her reflection. And in the reflection, for less than a second, the street is slightly different: a shutter open that is closed, a warm light in a window that is dark, and a figure under a pale blue umbrella who could be Mara, or could be no one.

It is gone.

Vera covers her face with her hands.

Above them, an elevated train passes, a long ribbon of lit windows. Inside, strangers sleep, read, stare at their phones. Nobody looks down.

Only now does the SCORE enter: sparse and mournful, as if coming from very far away.

The shot holds. Long enough that it becomes hard to watch. There is nothing Jack can say. Nothing that fixes it.

INT./EXT. VARIOUS - NIGHT - SERIES OF SHOTS

Still frames. No people.

-- A single red high-heeled shoe lying in a puddle on an empty street, rain dimpling the water around it.

-- The hotel lounge, empty, the chairs up. The pale blue umbrella still leaning against the bar stool.

-- The Hive at night, the noodle shop shutter down, its old sign still faintly glowing.

-- The vending machine on the empty street, humming, lit, waiting for no one.

-- A small television in a shop window, showing only static.

>CUT TO BLACK.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - NIGHT

Darkness. Rain on the window.

Vera sits on the floor with her back against the bed, still in the ruined red dress, mascara dried on her face. One shoe.

In her hand, the old steel lighter.

She opens it. Closes it. Opens it.

She should throw it away. She holds it against her chest instead, and bends over it, and cries without making a sound.

She still loves him. She hates herself for it.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - NIGHT

The desk lamp. Static on the TV. Jack sits in his wet coat at the desk. He still hasn't washed his hands.

On the desk: Daniel Voss's notebook.

He hears her voice. Over and over. Not the words from tonight. The words from the noodle counter at 11:40.

VERA (V.O.)
You're the first person I've trusted since she disappeared.

He opens the drawer. Takes out a clean envelope. Puts the notebook inside.

He picks up a pen to write something on the envelope. He holds it over the paper for a long time.

He writes nothing.

EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING, CORRIDOR - DAWN

Grey light. An open-air walkway along the third floor. Rain dripping from the railing.

Vera opens her door. She is still in the dress. She hasn't slept.

On the doormat: a plain envelope. No name.

She picks it up. Opens it. The cloth-covered notebook.

She sees the name inside the cover, and her whole body goes still.

DANIEL VOSS.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

Vera sits at the low table in the dawn light. Beside her, the two cups from the beginning of the film, both empty now. She turns the pages.

Her father's handwriting. Neat, slanted, careful.

DANIEL (V.O.)
Shiohama. Third visit. The residents say men came in the spring with flowers, and then in the summer with iron bars. The fire began in two places at once. Fires don't do that.

She turns pages. The handwriting grows faster.

DANIEL (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The claim will be paid. Everyone wants it paid. The company, the police, the man who owns the land now. Kurose. Always Kurose.

Pages.

DANIEL (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The police have given me a young detective who speaks English. They call him Jack. He's bright. He believes me. We ate noodles at Kaneko's and I told him everything and he wrote it all down.

Vera stops. Reads that line again.

Her hand goes to her mouth.

She turns the page. The line we didn't see Jack read, underlined twice.

DANIEL (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Today Jack signed the report. Accidental fire. I don't blame him. He is twenty-eight years old and they own his whole life. But I thought, of all of them, he would stand with me.

Vera stares at the page.

DANIEL (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I'll go on alone. I've done it before.

The last pages. The handwriting is almost unrecognisable now.

DANIEL (V.O.) (CONT'D)
They followed me home again tonight. The girls were asleep. I stood at the door a long time.
(beat)
If something happens to me, it will not be what they say. Tell Vera. When she is old enough. Tell her it will not be what they say.

Vera closes the notebook.

For twenty years she believed her father chose to leave her.

She sits in the grey light, holding the notebook against her chest, the way she held the lighter.

She has been given back her father and taken Jack away in the same hour. She doesn't know which to feel first.


INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - DAY

Rows of cluttered desks. Phones. The radio playing low somewhere. On the wall, the clock that runs a minute fast.

Ishida sits at his desk writing a report in careful longhand.

Jack walks the length of the room. Detectives look up and then look away. He hasn't shaved. There is still dried blood in the creases of his knuckles.

He stops at Ishida's desk. Ishida doesn't look up.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Nine o'clock. A grey car. Your driver.

Ishida finishes his sentence. Puts down the pen.

JACK (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Only you knew.

A long pause.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
You told me yourself, Jack.
(beat)
You always tell the wrong person.

Jack's hands close at his sides. The room has gone quiet around them.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Twenty years ago. Daniel. Was that you?

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
I have never killed anyone in my life.
(beat)
I only ever told people where to find them.

Jack looks at him for a long time. Everyone in the room is waiting for him to hit Ishida.

He doesn't.

ISHIDA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Where is it? Sakai's thing.

Jack turns and walks away down the long room, past the desks, past the clock.

Ishida watches him go. For the first time, he looks afraid.

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - DAY

The bar in daylight. Chairs on the tables. Okada behind the counter.

He sees Jack's face and his hands, and he doesn't ask. He opens the cash drawer, lifts out the tray, and hands Jack the cassette.

Jack holds it.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
The girl?

Jack can't answer.

Okada closes his eyes. Then he pours two small glasses and puts one in front of Jack. They drink together, without a toast.

INT. TOTO SHIMBUN NEWSROOM - DAY

An old newspaper office. Stacks of paper. Desks jammed together. Televisions on the walls showing three different channels. Nobody under fifty looks up from a screen.

In a glass-walled office at the back: HARADA (50s), the editor, grey-haired, sleeves rolled. On her desk, a framed photo of the JOURNALIST from the bar, laughing at some office party.

On the desk between them: an old cassette player, borrowed from somewhere, and the tape.

Harada presses PLAY.

Hiss. Then two men's voices, twenty years younger. Sakai's rough. The other one smooth, patient, faintly bored.

SAKAI (V.O.)
(in Japanese; recorded)
There are still people in the building. Old people. They won't sign.

KUROSE (V.O.)
(in Japanese; recorded)
The building must be empty by the end of the month.

SAKAI (V.O.)
(in Japanese; recorded)
And if it isn't?

KUROSE (V.O.)
(in Japanese; recorded)
Then it will be empty in a different way.
(beat)
Don't make me say it more clearly, Sakai. I don't like to repeat myself.

Harada stops the tape. The newsroom noise outside the glass seems very far away.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
That's Kurose.

JACK
(in Japanese)
That's Kurose.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
A voice on a twenty-year-old tape. His lawyers will say it's a fake. They'll say Sakai was a gangster with a grudge.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Then you'll need a witness.

She looks at him.

JACK (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Twenty years ago I was a police detective. An American insurance investigator named Daniel Voss proved the Shiohama fire was arson. I believed him. I was ordered to close the case, and I signed a report saying the fire was an accident.
(beat)
Weeks later he was found dead. I didn't ask any questions.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
You understand what you're saying. You'll be named. Your part too.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Start with my part.

Harada looks at him for a long moment. Then she looks at the photograph of her dead reporter on the desk. She takes a notebook from her drawer and opens it to a clean page.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
From the beginning.

Jack begins to talk. We don't hear it. We watch him through the glass wall of her office, among the busy desks and flickering televisions: a man, for the first time in twenty years, not silent.

INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAY

The fortieth floor. Rain on the glass. Tokyo grey and endless below.

Vera sits in a leather chair in front of Kurose's desk. She wears a plain dark coat. Her father's notebook is on her lap, her hands flat on its cover.

Kurose sits across from her. Courteous. Curious. He pours her tea himself.

KUROSE
When my secretary said the daughter of Daniel Voss wanted to see me, I didn't believe her.

His English is perfect. Old-fashioned.

KUROSE (CONT'D)
You have his eyes. He looked at people the same way. As if he expected them to tell the truth.

VERA
Did you?

KUROSE
To him? I don't remember.
(beat)
Your father was a good man, Miss Voss. I mean that sincerely. There are not many.
(beat)
Good men are very expensive.

Vera doesn't touch the tea.

KUROSE (CONT'D)
What is it you want? Money is vulgar. But it is also useful. For a young woman alone, in a foreign city.

VERA
I wanted to see your face.

KUROSE
And?

VERA
It's just a face.

For the first time, something flickers in him. Not fear. Irritation, perhaps, at being looked at like that.

Vera stands. She holds up the notebook. Not threatening. Just showing it to him.

VERA (CONT'D)
My father kept notes. He wrote your name on every page.
(beat)
And now I know.

She walks to the door. Stops beside the glass case with the model of the redevelopment inside. She looks down at it: the little white towers, the little plaza, the fountain where the Hive is.

VERA (CONT'D)
It's very clean.

She goes.

Kurose sits still for a moment. Then he presses a button on his desk phone.

KUROSE
(in Japanese; into phone)
Follow her.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

The bulb. The flour sacks. The futon, folded now.

Jack sits on the floor against the wall. He has been hiding here since the newspaper; he can't go home. His face is grey with exhaustion.

The curtain opens. Kaneko.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Someone for you.

She stands aside.

Vera.

Jack gets to his feet. Neither of them moves toward the other.

VERA
She asked me to come. Kaneko. She said I should see where Mara was.

She looks around the tiny room. The bare bulb. The flour sacks. And on the wall, taped up with rice-paper tape, pages from Mara's sketchbook: drawings of the noodle counter, but from the inside now. From behind the curtain. The back of a head on the third stool.

Vera walks to the wall. Looks at the drawing for a long time.

VERA (CONT'D)
That's me.

JACK
She drew it after you left.

VERA
She was here. The day I came.

JACK
Three feet away.

Vera touches the paper with one finger.

VERA
And you told her not to come out.

JACK
She told herself.
(beat)
She was protecting you. So was I. We were both wrong.

VERA
I read his notebook.

JACK
I know.

VERA
He didn't blame you.

JACK
I know.

VERA
I don't know if I'm as good as he was.

JACK
I'm not asking you to be.

Silence. A train passes overhead. The bulb swings.

And under the train, so quietly it's almost part of it: in the passage outside, a man's voice, murmuring into his sleeve.

MASKED MAN (O.S.)
(in Japanese)
Position.

Jack's head snaps round. Vera sees his face and understands.

The bulb goes on swinging.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - CONTINUOUS

Four masked men move through the narrow corridors in single file, weapons up. The passages are too narrow for anything else.

Doors that stood open close softly, one after another, as they pass. The Hive is watching them.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Kaneko pulls the shutter down with a crash. She turns off the fluorescent tube.

KANEKO
(in Japanese; to Jack)
Up. Through the back. The stairs by the dentist. All the way to the roof.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Come with us.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
I have lived here fifty years. They can come and find me.

She pushes them toward the back.

INT. THE HIVE, RADIO REPAIR SHOP - CONTINUOUS

The RADIO REPAIRMAN looks up from his bench at the sound of boots in the corridor. He looks at the old fuse box on his wall.

He reaches up and pulls the main switch.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - CONTINUOUS

DARK.

Every bulb in the building goes out at once.

The masked men stop. Flashlights snap on, tight white beams in the narrow corridors, catching dripping pipes, closed doors, laundry, faces at windows that vanish the moment the light touches them.

The Hive knows its own dark. The men don't.

INT. THE HIVE, STAIRWELL - CONTINUOUS

Pitch black. Vera and Jack climbing a narrow concrete stair by touch. Her hand on the wall. His hand finding hers in the dark.

She lets him.

Below them, a flashlight beam sweeps the bottom of the stairwell. They freeze.

Somewhere a DOG starts barking. Then a baby cries. Then a radio, somewhere, turned up very loud: an old ballad. The one from the neighbour's wall.

Then another radio. Then a television. Then someone banging a pot with a spoon.

The whole building starts to make noise, on purpose, all at once. The flashlight swings away, confused.

Jack and Vera climb.

EXT. THE HIVE, ROOFTOP - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Wind. Water tanks, television aerials, laundry poles, pigeon cages. The whole forest of the Hive's roof, and beyond it, Tokyo in every direction, lit and indifferent.

At the edge, very close, the elevated railway: a narrow maintenance walkway running beside the tracks, separated from the roof by a gap of a metre and a low fence.

Jack helps Vera over the gap. She has one hand in his. She jumps. He follows.

EXT. RAILWAY MAINTENANCE WALKWAY - CONTINUOUS

A narrow steel walkway beside the tracks. Behind them, a door bangs open on the Hive's roof. Flashlight beams sweep the aerials and water tanks.

And ahead, the rails begin to sing. A light grows at the far end of the viaduct.

A train.

Jack pulls Vera flat against the fence at the edge of the walkway. There is nowhere else to go.

The train arrives. A roaring wall of noise and wind and lit windows, a metre from their faces, strobing across them. Passengers inside reading, sleeping, looking at their phones. None of them see.

Vera and Jack are pressed together against the fence, faces inches apart, rain and train-light washing over them.

She doesn't pull away this time.

On the Hive's roof, the flashlight beams search the tracks. The train stands between them and the walkway, carriage after carriage.

When the last carriage passes, the walkway is empty.

EXT. STREET BELOW THE VIADUCT - MOMENTS LATER

Vera and Jack come down a steel maintenance ladder into an empty street. Soaked. Breathing hard.

Behind them, the Hive: every window lit again now, every radio playing, every resident awake. In the distance, sirens.

Vera steps away from him. Just one step. Enough.

They look at each other in the rain. There is too much to say, and none of it can be said tonight.

VERA
Is Kaneko --

JACK
The Hive looks after its own.

She nods. She looks up at the building full of light.

VERA
Mara was safe here. Until us.

He has no answer to that. She doesn't need one.

EXT. POLICE STATION - NIGHT

Rain. Ishida comes down the front steps without an umbrella.

At the kerb, a black sedan. Engine running. Wipers beating slowly.

He stops. He knows this car.

A long moment. Then the rear door opens from inside.

INT. BLACK SEDAN, BACK SEAT - CONTINUOUS

Warm amber light. Leather. The rain is suddenly very far away.

Kurose sits in the back, impeccable, a small steel flask in his hands. He does not look at Ishida. He pours tea into the flask's cup.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
Get in, Ishida. You'll catch cold.

Ishida gets in. The door closes. The sound of the rain becomes a soft drumming on the roof.

The car pulls away.

Kurose offers him the cup. Ishida looks at it.

KUROSE (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
It's only tea.

Ishida takes it. Doesn't drink.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
I did everything you asked. For twenty years.

KUROSE
(in Japanese)
Yes. You were always very careful.
(beat)
That's why I trusted you. And that's why you understand.

Ishida looks out of the window. Tokyo slides past in the rain: a lit vending machine, a closed noodle shop, an elevated train full of sleeping strangers.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Where are we going?

Kurose doesn't answer. He simply looks ahead, as if the question was impolite.

Ishida nods, slowly. He understands.

He lifts the cup, and drinks the tea.

EXT. TOKYO STREET - CONTINUOUS

The black car recedes down a long wet road, its taillights smearing red, exactly like the car in the first scene of the film.

It turns a corner. Gone.

INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - MORNING

Grey daylight. A cardboard box on Ishida's desk. A young detective is clearing it.

He opens the bottom drawer. Empty.

On the wall, the clock still runs a minute fast.

EXT. THE HIVE - MORNING

Rain.

In front of the Hive, a white ceremonial tent. Rows of folding chairs. A podium. Officials in dark suits. A giant banner of the computer rendering: glass towers, the little plaza, the fountain. TOMORROW'S TOKYO. A silver shovel on a stand, tied with a red-and-white ribbon, waiting for the ground-breaking.

Across the street, a small electronics shop. In its window, a row of televisions, old CRTs and new flat screens side by side, all showing the same morning news: a photograph of Kurose, and a front page of the Toto Shimbun held up to the camera.

People on the pavement slow down to watch. Then stop.

Among them, beside Kaneko, under a plain umbrella: Vera.

A black car pulls up at the tent. An AIDE hurries round with a large umbrella and opens the rear door.

Kurose steps out. Immaculate. He buttons his jacket. He turns toward the podium.

Four men in plain dark suits are standing between him and it. PROSECUTORS. One of them holds up an identification card and says something we can't hear.

Kurose looks at them. For a moment, nothing happens at all.

Then the lead prosecutor gestures toward a plain grey car at the kerb.

The aide steps forward with the umbrella. The prosecutor shakes his head, very slightly.

The aide lowers it.

Kurose walks from the tent to the grey car. Twenty metres. In the rain. No umbrella.

The rain soaks his silver hair flat. It darkens the shoulders of his beautiful suit. By the time he reaches the car, he looks like what he is: an old man.

Cameras flash. The CRTs in the shop window show the same moment, a second behind, over and over.

Vera watches the whole twenty metres. She does not look away.

Kaneko takes Vera's hand.

Further down the street, alone, collar up: Jack. Watching too.

Vera sees him. He sees her.

Across the street, through the rain and the camera flashes, neither of them moves.

The grey car pulls away. Behind it, the silver shovel stands on its stand, untouched, its ribbon going dark in the rain.

EXT. ROOFTOP OF JACK'S BUILDING - DAY

Days later. The rain has stopped for the first time in the film. The sky is pale and washed and enormous.

A small flat roof: laundry poles, a water tank, a single potted plant someone has kept alive. Below, the elevated railway, and the trains going past at eye level.

Jack stands at the railing. He hears the door behind him.

Vera. In a plain coat. Her hair dry.

She comes to stand beside him at the railing. Not close. Not far.

VERA
Harada says the prosecutors want you to testify.

JACK
Yes.

VERA
And your licence?

JACK
Gone.
(beat)
It should have gone twenty years ago.

A train passes below. They watch it.

Jack takes something from his pocket. Holds it out on his open palm.

The red bird clip.

JACK (CONT'D)
This is yours.

Vera looks at it. She takes it.

JACK (CONT'D)
She said your father gave it to her. She said you only claim it was yours.

Vera laughs. It comes out broken.

VERA
Liar. It was mine.

She closes her hand around it.

Jack looks at the trains. It is the hardest thing he will ever say, and he says it simply.

JACK
At the end, she asked me to tell you something.

Vera goes very still.

JACK (CONT'D)
She said to tell you she was sorry.

Vera stares at him.

And then she understands. Not the words. What they mean. The fight. The last cruel things she said at the door. The flight home. Everything she has carried since the first scene.

Mara wasn't angry. Mara had forgiven her the whole time.

Vera turns away to the railing. Her shoulders shake. Jack doesn't touch her. He stands beside her while she cries, the way he knelt beside her in the rain. Close enough. Not closer.

When she can speak:

VERA
You could have told me that in the rain.

JACK
I couldn't say anything in the rain.

VERA
No.
(beat)
Neither could I.

A train. They watch it pass.

VERA (CONT'D)
I don't know what we are.

JACK
Neither do I.

VERA
I still have your lighter.

JACK
I know.

She takes it from her coat pocket. Looks at it. Opens it. Closes it.

She doesn't give it back. She puts it away again.

VERA
Kaneko's opening a new place. Near the station, under the arches. She's taking the sign. And the stools.
(beat)
She says the third one's still mine.

She walks to the rooftop door. Stops. Doesn't look back.

VERA (CONT'D)
She says she opens at six.

She goes.

Jack stands alone at the railing. A train passes, its windows full of people. For a moment, in one of the windows, the reflection of his own face.

EXT. THE HIVE - DAY

Weeks later.

The Hive is coming down.

Excavators bite into the walls with long steel jaws. Concrete falls in slow grey curtains. Dust hangs in the air.

The building has been cut open like the illustrated cross-sections in an old book. Rooms stand exposed to the sky, stacked one above another: a wall of flowered wallpaper, a calendar still pinned beside a window, a mirror, a child's height marks pencilled on a doorframe.

The camera tracks slowly sideways along the ruined face of the building, as it tracked along the lit windows of the living one. Empty room after empty room. We remember who lived in each.

At the barrier on the street, a small crowd watches. The radio repairman. The family. The girl with the violin case.

Kaneko stands among them, holding the old noodle-shop sign against her chest, wrapped in a blanket.

INT. KANEKO'S NEW COUNTER - NIGHT

A tiny place in a brick railway arch near the station. Six new stools, the same height as the old ones. Steam. One warm bulb. A small radio on the shelf, playing low.

Above the counter, the old hand-painted sign. Faded. Unmistakable.

Kaneko works the pot with long chopsticks.

Vera sits on the third stool. A bowl in front of her. The red bird clip in her hair.

A train passes overhead. The bulb trembles. The steam shivers. Nobody looks up.

On the radio, the old ballad begins. The one from the neighbour's wall.

Vera eats.

Behind her, the door opens.

Cool blue street light spills across the floor. And into it, a long shadow falls: a man in a coat, standing in the doorway, his shadow stretching all the way across the floor to the foot of her stool.

Vera sees the shadow. She stops eating.

She doesn't turn.

Kaneko looks up at the door. Then at Vera. Then, without a word, she takes down a second bowl and sets it on the counter in front of the fourth stool.

Vera looks at the second bowl.

HOLD on the back of her head, the red clip, the steam, the shadow on the floor.

She doesn't turn.

>CUT TO BLACK.

Over black: a train passing. Rain beginning again, softly.

>THE END<
